newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-B.A.T gains after U.S. court ruling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-B.A.T gains after U.S. court ruling.

text.p: Shares in B.A.T Industries Plc rose in early trade on Tuesday after a U.S. court cleared R.J. Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco, of responsibility for the death of Jean Connor, a smoker who died of lung cancer.

The late Monday decision added to B.A.T's confidence that it can overturn on appeal the case of Grady Carter, awarded $750,000 by a Florida jury last year, against its American tobacco unit Brown & Williamson. The Carter case was bought by Norwood "Woody" Wilner, the same lawyer who bought the Connor family lawsuit.
"I think it reinforces our belief that the Carter verdict will ultimately be reversed," a company spokesman said.

U.S. tobacco shares rose sharply after the verdict, B.A.T was quoted up 16-1/2p at 536 at midday. On Wall Street, Philip Morris Cos Inc on Monday rose $3-7/8 to $44 and RJR Nabisco gained $3 to $32-5/8.

The Florida jury found that Reynolds was not negligent, in a closely-watched wrongful death verdict that could strengthen the industry's position in talks with a group of state attorneys aimed at settling litigation and other issues.

However the state attorneys said the Florida verdict would not affect their talks with the tobacco industry, arguing that it applied to an individual case and would not affect their attempt to recoup public costs of treating smoking-related illnesses.

The B.A.T spokesman declined comment on the industry's negotiations with U.S. state attorneys. The industry faces a string of lawsuits in America, including 24 so-called Medicaid cases bought by individual states to recover funds spent on treating patients with tobacco related ailments.
The first state attorney case, bought by Mississippi, is due to be heard on July 7.

The industry has never had damages upheld at the end of the appeal process in over 500 cases filed since 1954, but tobacco companies are acutely aware they cannot win the public relations war against the increasingly powerful health lobby in the major industrial nations.
B.A.T chairman Lord Cairn acknowledged in April that the company must brace itself for some reversals, especially at the lower court level.

Legislators are also turning more hostile towards the industry, imposing restrictions on the use of advertising. In New York the city council is seeking to ban cigarette and smokeless tobacco advertising and promotion within 1,000 feet of schools with other cities including Washington D.C. and Seattle to follow suit.
Britain's new Labour Party, which swept to a landslide election victory last week, has pledged to ban all tobacco advertising.
Imperial Tobacco Plc, the UK's other tobacco stock, was up 6-1/2p at 406 at midday, though it has no direct presence in the U.S. market.
